short: The World Bank's 2024 calendar-year estimates put 2.29% of Indians below $3 a day and 78.78% below $8.30, in 2021 PPP prices. Direct survey-year readings differ.
About 76.5% of Indians lie between those lines in the report's binned 2024 distribution. A low extreme-poverty rate does not establish economic security or adequate nutrition.
Survey redesign, PPP revisions and welfare imputation affect measurement. Comparing different poverty lines cannot isolate a questionnaire effect.
The combined jobs counterfactual lowers $8.30 poverty by 22.17 percentage points. It is an accounting exercise, not a forecast or a causal policy estimate.
macha: India has made a large dent in extreme poverty. That still leaves most households below the higher benchmark used for upper-middle-income countries. The distinction matters for a family trying to pay for healthcare or survive a spell without work. Poor paid workers already put in about 44 hours a week. The question is what those hours buy them, and how much of their security a consumption survey can actually see.

article.title: What does the World Bank's 2026 poverty report actually show about India, and why do economists still disagree?
article.standfirst: India's estimated extreme poverty rate fell to 2.29% in 2024. Yet 78.78% remained below $8.30 a day. The World Bank's new tables show how both can be true, and where survey changes, welfare valuation and jobs simulations need a more careful reading.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## Why is 'Has India ended extreme poverty?' the wrong question to ask in 2026?

India's poverty story changes with the line you draw. In the World Bank's *Poverty, Prosperity, and Planet Report 2026*, the estimated share living below $3 a person a day fell from 49.38% in 1990 to **2.29% in 2024**. At $8.30 a day, 78.78% remained below the line. Both estimates come from the same consumption distribution. One records the retreat of extreme poverty; the other records how far most households remain from the living standards used to assess poverty in upper-middle-income countries.

These are purchasing-power-parity dollars, or PPP dollars. They compare what money buys across countries. They are not dollars converted at the rupee exchange rate. The $3 line is based on national poverty lines in low-income countries. Crossing it does not establish adequate nutrition, secure work or protection against a medical bill.

The report's calendar-year estimates are also different from direct survey readings. Its `Country_FGT` series aligns surveys to common years using national-accounts growth. India's latest direct survey is the Household Consumption Expenditure Survey (HCES) 2023-24, recorded as 2023 in the Poverty and Inequality Platform (PIP). It puts poverty at 2.57% below $3, 16.12% below $4.20 and 79.98% below $8.30. The report's lined-up estimates for 2024 are 2.29%, 14.88% and 78.78%, respectively. The 2026 and 2030 figures extend those distributions forward; they are estimates, not new household interviews.

At the extreme line, the historical change is large. Lined-up poverty fell from 49.38% in 1990 to 28.51% in 2011 and 2.29% in 2024, when about 33 million people remained below $3 a day. The 2026 nowcast is 1.40%. At the $4.20 lower-middle-income line, the corresponding rates were 77.29%, 59.39% and 14.88%, leaving about 216 million people below the line in 2024. At $8.30, the decline was much slower: from 97.08% in 1990 to 93.08% in 2011 and 78.78% in 2024, or about 1.14 billion people.

The World Bank's own India brief, published in October 2026, projects a slower decline. It puts the share below $4.20 at 14.2% in 2026, falling to 12.1% by 2028, against 10.24% for 2026 in the report's lineup. The two come from different models. The report's nowcasts apply real per-capita GDP growth from *Global Economic Prospects*, June 2026, assume that everyone's income grows at the same rate, and pass 0.7 of that growth through to consumption-based estimates such as India's. The brief calls its figures "indicative microsimulation-based projections" that will be updated as labour-market and macroeconomic data are revised, and does not set out the model. Neither is a measurement. A gap of about four points between two World Bank estimates for the same year shows how much a projection depends on its assumptions.

The space between those lines contains most of the country. The report's 1,000-bin distribution puts **76.5% of Indians between $3 and $8.30 a day in 2024**. Reduce every bin's real consumption by a hypothetical 10%, then count again. The share below $4.20 rises from 14.9% to 23.2%; at $3 it rises from 2.3% to 4.4%, and at $8.30 from 78.8% to 85.1%. This static exercise shows the thin buffer above each cutoff. It does not predict a shock or track which families will fall back into poverty. Both endpoints use the same bins, which approximate the national lineup and resolve to about 0.1 percentage point.

The poverty gap adds depth to that count. Divide the population-average shortfall by the share below the line, and the result is the average shortfall among poor people. In the direct HCES 2023-24 PIP estimates, consumption among those below $3 averages about 13.2% short of that line. At $4.20 the shortfall is 15.9%; at $8.30 it is 34.1%. The higher line captures a much deeper average deficit, not merely more households just below a cutoff. These ratios are approximate because the API inputs are rounded.

A separate measure lets the poverty line rise with domestic living standards. Under the World Bank's 2021 PPP method, the Societal Poverty Line is `max($3.00, $1.30 + 0.5 × national median daily consumption)`. For India, the line was $3.23 in 2011-12 and $4.27 in 2023-24. The share below it fell from 33.44% to 17.35%. The hero chart shows this survey-year series alongside the three calendar-year lines, so its dates and estimation basis differ.

The **Prosperity Gap** answers another question. For each person, divide the $28-a-day prosperity standard by their daily consumption, then average those ratios across everyone. Poorer people contribute more to the score because their ratios are larger. This is not $28 divided by average consumption, and a national score of five does not mean multiplying everyone's spending by five would bring everyone to $28.

India's survey-based Prosperity Gap fell from 9.70 in 1993 to 7.67 in 2011, 5.36 in 2022 and 4.95 in 2023. The state map shows how unevenly that shortfall is distributed. Using the Global Subnational Atlas of Poverty's 2023 reference year, Jharkhand's score is 6.72, Chhattisgarh's 6.31 and Odisha's 5.92. Kerala is at 3.91, Goa at 3.16 and Chandigarh at 2.22. These are population averages of individual ratios, not uniform growth targets for each state's residents.

Young children face another disadvantage within those states. In the report's separate Subnational Poverty and Inequality Database (SPID), the share of children aged 0-5 living in households below $8.30 is higher than the all-age share in every state and union territory. In Kerala, the comparison is 75.8% against 58.5%; in Maharashtra, 91.0% against 82.0%. The chart shows selected states. These groups overlap: the all-age population includes the children. The measure describes the household consumption available per person, not what a child eats or receives within the home.

The brief adds the rural-urban split for HCES 2023-24 at $4.20: 19.3% of rural Indians and 8.6% of urban Indians were below the line. It warns that the survey weights are anchored in the 2011 Census frame, so the survey likely understates the current urban share of the population. It also describes poverty as increasingly concentrated: households in a contiguous belt from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal account for about 57% of India's poor population.

## How did a 2021 PPP price revision and a new survey questionnaire rewrite the numbers?

A poverty estimate depends on what households report, how that spending is valued and where the line is set. India's recent estimates changed on all these fronts. The disputes are easier to follow when those changes are kept separate.

### India's own poverty line stopped in 2011-12

India has no current official poverty line. The last official estimate is the Planning Commission's for 2011-12, made with the Tendulkar method: 21.9% of the population, down from 45.3% in 1993-94. The next national consumption survey, for 2017-18, was withheld, officially for data-quality reasons. Leaked findings reported in November 2019 said real average spending per person had fallen 3.7% since 2011-12, with rural spending down 8.8% and urban spending up 2%. The next published survey, HCES 2022-23, used a new design.

Where the line sits has been disputed for decades. A 1979 task force led by Y.K. Alagh tied it to food energy: the spending at which people typically consumed 2,400 kcal a day in rural areas and 2,100 kcal in urban areas. The Lakdawala expert group, appointed in 1989, reported in 1993 and kept that line. The Tendulkar expert group, reporting in 2009, did not construct a new line; it adopted the officially measured 2004-05 urban line and converted it to a different recall period. In September 2011 the Planning Commission told the Supreme Court that, at June 2011 prices, the line was Rs 965 per person a month in urban areas and Rs 781 in rural areas, about Rs 32 and Rs 26 a day. The figure became shorthand for a line that seemed to describe destitution rather than poverty.

For 2011-12 the Tendulkar lines were Rs 816 per person a month in rural India and Rs 1,000 in urban India. The Rangarajan expert group, reporting in 2014, recomputed requirements for calories, proteins and fats, added essential non-food spending, and set Rs 972 and Rs 1,407. On the same survey its line put 29.5% of Indians below it. That line was never adopted. A NITI Aayog task force reported in 2016 that a consensus for either the Tendulkar line or a higher one did not emerge, and recommended another expert committee. No national line has been set since, so every recent Indian poverty rate is an estimate on someone's chosen line.

### The PPP revision changed the yardstick

The World Bank adopted the 2021 PPP poverty lines in June 2025. The old lines of $2.15, $3.65 and $6.85 in 2017 PPP became $3, $4.20 and $8.30 in 2021 PPP. Comparing the two PPP vintages within the frozen September 2026 PIP release holds the release and survey year fixed.

For HCES 2023-24, the extreme-poverty estimate changes from 1.02% at the old $2.15 line to 2.57% at the new $3 line. At the lower-middle-income benchmark, the estimate goes the other way, from 19.91% at $3.65 to 16.12% at $4.20. At the upper-middle-income benchmark, it moves from 79.81% to 79.98%.

The dollar amounts belong to different price bases. Their percentage changes alone do not tell us how much stricter each line became in India. PPPs, domestic price adjustments and the underlying national poverty lines all matter. These revisions change the measuring rule; they do not describe households suddenly gaining or losing consumption.

PIP uses one national consumption PPP factor for India, Rs 19.47 per international dollar in 2021 prices. The frozen national series does not contain separate rural and urban PPP conversion factors. Rural and urban comparisons require attention to the spatial price adjustments in the welfare aggregate, rather than invented sector-specific PPPs.

### The survey changed too

HCES 2022-23 and 2023-24 collect the food, consumables and services, and durables modules over three monthly visits, rather than the earlier single-visit schedule. Longer item lists and changes in fieldwork can change how much spending households recall. A cleaner questionnaire is valuable, but it complicates comparison with an older survey.

PIP records the break formally. Its comparability field puts India's surveys in separate groups: 1977, 1983 and 1987 each stand alone, 1993-94 to 2009-10 form one comparable run, 2011-12 stands alone, and 2022-23 to 2023-24 form another. The charts here draw each survey as a dot and join surveys from different groups only with a thin grey link. The October 2026 India brief is less strict in words. It calls the 2011-12, 2022-23 and 2023-24 surveys "broadly comparable, despite several key improvements", but adds that the large welfare gains between 2022-23 and 2023-24 "likely reflect both genuine welfare gains and better measurement".

Himanshu, Peter Lanjouw and Philipp Schirmer examine that break in Tinbergen Institute Discussion Paper TI 2025-069/V. They use survey-to-survey imputation to estimate consumption on a more consistent historical basis. Their models do not measure an alternative truth directly; they depend on the stability of relationships between consumption and the characteristics used to predict it.

The chart deliberately shows several poverty lines as well as several survey treatments. Direct HCES yields 2.35% at the old $2.15 line and 5.25% at the new $3 line. Applying the Rangarajan line directly gives 7.2%. The paper's CES-based Tendulkar estimates range from 11.3% to 13.6%; its EUS-to-PLFS Tendulkar estimates include 17.5%, 18.3% and 19.9%. Under the Rangarajan-equivalent MMRP line, the sector-wide EUS-to-PLFS model gives 25.9%.

That spread cannot be attributed entirely to the questionnaire. It combines different poverty lines, recall concepts and models. The useful comparisons hold the line fixed while changing the survey treatment. Standard errors and model assumptions matter too; this chart is not a confidence interval for India's poverty rate.

### Who says poverty has nearly vanished?

The same data feed sharply different public claims. Surjit Bhalla, Karan Bhasin and Arvind Virmani, in an IMF working paper in April 2022, put extreme poverty at $1.90 a day in 2011 PPP at 0.8% in 2019, counting in-kind food transfers. After the HCES 2022-23 factsheet appeared in February 2024, NITI Aayog's chief executive said the survey indicated poverty below 5%. SBI Research, using HCES 2023-24, put rural poverty at 4.86% and urban poverty at 4.09%. Each uses its own line and its own treatment of transfers, so these numbers cannot be lined up against each other or against the World Bank's.

The World Bank has been on both sides of the argument. In 2022, Sutirtha Sinha Roy and Roy van der Weide used the private Consumer Pyramids Household Survey to estimate extreme poverty at 10.2% in 2019, down from 22.5% in 2011. Jean Drèze and Anmol Somanchi argued that poor households were grossly under-represented in that survey. The 2026 report says the Consumer Pyramids-based estimates for 2015 to 2021 have been removed from PIP because of concerns about comparability with the government's new survey. India therefore has no PIP survey points between 2011-12 and 2022-23.

None of these estimates finds that poverty rose between 2011-12 and the 2020s, although the withheld 2017-18 survey suggested spending fell for a time. The dispute is over how far and how fast poverty fell, and how much of the measured fall comes from changes in measurement.

### Free goods count as consumption, with limits

MoSPI publishes HCES spending with and without the imputed value of specified goods received free through welfare programmes. Foodgrain and items such as uniforms or bicycles have consumption value even when the household pays nothing for them. This is distinct from a cash transfer or market earnings.

In the official HCES 2023-24 press note, average monthly per-capita spending rises from **Rs 4,122 to Rs 4,247 in rural India** when these items are included, a Rs 125 increase, or about 3.0%. In urban India it rises from Rs 6,996 to Rs 7,078, a Rs 82 increase, or about 1.2%. Those are sector averages; they cannot establish the boost for the poorest households or how much poverty would change without transfers.

The boundary matters. MoSPI does not impute the value of free health services or waived education fees in these estimates, because their value is difficult to establish through household recall. Consumption with welfare imputation therefore still excludes some public services. Nor is MoSPI's published with-imputation distribution identical to the World Bank's harmonised welfare aggregate, which makes its own adjustments for international poverty measurement.

### The survey and National Accounts tell different growth stories

In PIP, India's consumption Gini falls from 28.78 in 2011-12 to 25.51 in 2022-23 and 23.00 in 2023-24. The richest survey decile's share of consumption falls from 24.80% to 20.52% over the same endpoints. These describe measured consumption, not the distribution of income or wealth.

Those figures have been used for a larger claim. In July 2025 a Press Information Bureau backgrounder cited a Gini of 25.5 to call India "the fourth most equal country in the world", after the Slovak Republic, Slovenia and Belarus. Critics, including Alt News, pointed out that India's Gini measures consumption while the countries it was ranked against mostly report income, which is usually more unequal. The October 2026 India brief says the surveys may not fully capture the consumption of wealthier households and are likely to understate inequality.

The two latest HCES rounds offer a cleaner comparison because PIP explicitly marks 2022-23 and 2023-24 as comparable. Average real consumption grows 13.1% for the poorest surveyed tenth, against a measured decline of 2.9% for the richest surveyed tenth. The national mean rises 4.7%. This helps explain the falling consumption Gini within these rounds. Each decile contains different people at each date, however, and the survey's coverage of affluent households still matters. The result cannot establish that rich Indians as a whole became poorer.

Index the available series to 1977 and the divergence becomes clear. Real GDP per capita grows 5.70-fold by 2023, National Accounts household consumption per capita grows 4.49-fold, and survey mean consumption grows 2.09-fold. Each line is indexed from its own starting value; their original currency units are not placed on one scale.

This discrepancy warrants scrutiny. It does not, by itself, prove that missing rich households explain the whole gap or that National Accounts supply the correct distribution. Coverage, valuation, reporting errors and survey design can all contribute. The chart cannot tell us how to allocate the missing consumption across households. [Consumption inequality](/articles/income-inequality/) is only one part of the larger inequality question.

Wages tell a slower story still. Arindam Das and Jean Drèze, using the Labour Bureau's village wage series, estimate real wage growth of 0.8% a year between 2014-15 and 2023-24 for male agricultural labourers, and describe a "virtual stagnation" of real wages over the decade. The India brief reports that employment rose by about 134 million between 2017 and 2023, nearly twice the growth of the working-age population, largely as rural women entered paid work, while real earnings remained broadly unchanged. More earners per household is one way consumption can rise while wages do not; transfers and survey design are others. These sources cannot apportion the gap between them.

## Why do working Indians stay poor even when they work 44 hours a week?

The World Bank's jobs chapter makes a useful distinction between having work and earning enough from it. Its tables also use different poverty thresholds. The working-hours comparison uses $3 a day; most of the employment and education comparisons use $8.30. Mixing them would change who counts as poor halfway through an argument.

Among paid employees in households below $3 a day, average weekly hours are **44.05**, against 44.95 above the line. Among self-employed and unpaid workers, the corresponding figures are 37.05 and 40.61 hours. These are averages among people already working, not among all adults. Hours alone clearly cannot account for the difference in household consumption.

At the $8.30 line, the share of workers in poor households without secondary education falls from 86.71% in 2003 to 56.47% in 2024. Yet the share of working-age adults employed in those households falls from 60.72% to 58.29%. Among non-poor households, employment rises from 50.25% to 57.58%. These comparisons do not track the same families over time: households can move between poverty groups. They also do not isolate the effects of schooling, women's participation or age composition.

Job structure differs sharply. In 2024, 58.24% of workers in households below $8.30 are self-employed, against 45.24% above the line. Agriculture employs 45.92% of poor workers and 24.77% of non-poor workers. These descriptive differences help explain why [the quality of employment](/articles/how-many-good-jobs-is-india-creating/) matters alongside the employment rate. They do not establish the causal return from moving a particular worker into another job.

The report also supplies an accounting counterfactual. In its combined employment-and-worker-earnings scenario, India's $8.30 poverty rate falls from 78.78% to 56.61%, a **22.17 percentage-point reduction**. The poverty gap at that line, which averages the shortfall across the whole population as a share of the line, falls from 25.73% to 16.64%. At $3, the simulated headcount falls from 2.28% to 1.14%. The tiny difference between this baseline and the chapter-one 2.29% figure comes from separate replication outputs; we keep each as supplied.

That is a large simulated change, but it still leaves more than half the population below $8.30. It is not a forecast, a costed programme or proof that one particular jobs policy would deliver those gains. The processed counterfactual file gives combined results; it does not identify India's education-versus-sector contribution to the 22.17-point reduction.

## What questions about Indian poverty can still not be answered?

Money and capability do not move in lockstep. In the World Bank's multidimensional measure for HCES 2022-23, 17.74% of Indians are poor, against 5.25% below the monetary extreme line in the same survey. Sanitation deprivation affects 29.60%, lack of an adult with completed primary schooling 13.82%, drinking-water deprivation 6.39% and electricity deprivation 1.02%. These overlapping deprivations cannot be added together.

Even the headline for that measure differs between World Bank publications. The October 2026 India brief prints 15.5% for the same survey, while the report's MPM file used here gives 17.74%, with the same component rates after rounding. NITI Aayog's index has a different limit. Its widely quoted estimate that 24.82 crore people escaped multidimensional poverty in the nine years to 2022-23 runs from an estimated 2013-14 rate of 29.17% to a projected 2022-23 rate of 11.28%. Neither endpoint is a survey reading.

Nutrition provides a different lens, with a different denominator and date. The fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), conducted in 2019-21, found 35.5% of children under five stunted and 32.1% underweight. These are not percentages of all Indians or new findings from HCES 2023-24. The World Bank's multidimensional measure excludes nutrition and health, so it cannot stand in for them either.

Medical spending exposes another limit of expenditure measures. A household can finance treatment by borrowing or selling assets; the expenditure records consumption while the financing damages its balance sheet. The World Bank's financial-protection series for **2022** reports 30.94% facing financial hardship from out-of-pocket health spending, including 22.27% facing impoverishing spending. These are separate health-financing indicators, not the percentage pushed below this article's $3 line by one hospital bill.

HCES also samples households anew rather than following the same families year after year. It cannot measure how often a particular family falls back into poverty after a crop failure or an illness. Dividing household consumption by household size also leaves the allocation of food and healthcare within the home out of view.

The report's planet chapter adds environmental exposure, but its supplied exposure workbooks give regional and income-group aggregates. They cannot support an India state-level heat-or-flood poverty overlay. Presenting South Asia's exposure as India's would create a geographical error. That is a reporting gap to fill with compatible local hazard and household data.

The international comparison becomes less flattering at a higher line. In the common 2024 estimates, 78.8% of Indians are below $8.30 a day, against 68.5% in Bangladesh, 68.1% in Indonesia and 18.2% in Viet Nam; Pakistan is at 87.2%. India has a lower $3 poverty share than Bangladesh and Indonesia, but a higher share below $8.30. These are selected Asian comparators, not one income group. Indonesia's observation is marked actual; the other four are projections or lineup estimates, so the common year is not a common survey date.

India's role in global poverty changes with the benchmark too. In the chapter-one 2024 tables, India accounts for 4.03% of the world's population below $3, 14.56% below $4.20 and 30.42% below $8.30. In the separate 2026 table, it contributes 18.49% of the Global Prosperity Gap, against 18.31% of world population. The latter compares average welfare ratios, not a count of people below $28. A small share of global extreme poverty and a large share of the world's wider consumption shortfall can coexist.

Counted in people, India ranked fifth at $3 a day in 2024, with about 33 million below the line, behind Nigeria (95 million), the Democratic Republic of Congo (90 million), Pakistan (56 million) and Ethiopia (42 million). At $4.20 it ranks first, with about 216 million people. The report notes that India appears among the economies with the most extremely poor people because it is the most populous country in the world, not because its extreme-poverty rate is high.

## How to read these numbers: methodology and caveats

The frozen sources are the World Bank's 2026 report reproducibility package, FR_WLD_2026_763, the September 2026 PIP releases in both PPP vintages, MoSPI's HCES 2023-24 press note, the Tinbergen paper, NFHS-5 and the World Bank's 2022 health-financing observations. The package contains four chapters. Its processed tables can be audited without treating them as household-level raw microdata.

The November 2026 additions draw on the World Bank's October 2026 India brief, the first chapter of the 2026 report for the nowcast method and the Consumer Pyramids removal, the Planning Commission's 2013 press note and the Rangarajan-Dev monograph for India's poverty-line history, and the published positions in the measurement debate. Each is frozen with its hash in a separate follow-up folder. Statements by governments, banks and researchers are reported as their claims, not as estimates this article reproduces.

The three national trajectories use `Country_FGT`, with all annual observations from 1990 to 2030. Estimates after 2024 are drawn dashed. The societal-poverty series uses direct survey-year PIP observations, not the calendar-year lineup. Binned consumption values are approximate locations in the distribution; bin-based shares resolve only to a tenth of a percentage point.

The state figures use the `Data 2023` sheet of `AM26_GSAP_data.xlsx`. They are tied to HCES 2023-24 and the atlas's 2023 reference year. The `Data 2024` sheet applies a later lineup and should not be substituted without relabelling. State poverty shares are multiplied by 100 to convert proportions to percentages. Prosperity Gap values remain ratios.

The child comparison stays entirely within SPID's direct HCES survey estimates, labelled year 2023 and reference year 2023.58 in the workbook. The same-state rows use age groups `0-5` and `ALL`; the latter includes the former. Those estimates are distinct from the GSAP calendar lineup used for the state map and must not be substituted for it. No national child headcount is inferred from state percentages without compatible population weights.

The decile-growth calculation multiplies each national mean by that decile's consumption share and divides by 0.1, then computes the percentage change between the two comparable rounds. The consumption-loss exercise multiplies every 2024 bin's welfare by 0.9, keeps its population weight fixed and recomputes the share below each line. It assumes an equal proportional loss, and represents neither a forecast nor the effect of 10% price inflation. The Asian comparison uses `Country_FGT` at all three common lines in 2024, retaining each country's actual/projection flag.

For a rough rupee illustration, PIP's national 2021 PPP factor of Rs 19.47 multiplied by its unrounded 2023 consumer-price ratio gives about Rs 22.55 per PPP dollar in survey-year prices. Using 365/12 days per month, $3 is roughly Rs 68 a day or Rs 2,060 a month; $4.20 is Rs 95 a day or Rs 2,880 a month; $8.30 is Rs 187 a day or Rs 5,700 a month. These are national price equivalents, not separate rural and urban budgets or recommended spending minima.

The welfare-imputation chart uses only published sector averages. Its boost is `(with imputation − without imputation) / without imputation × 100`. A previous reconstruction by consumption fractile could not be independently reproduced from the frozen story files and has been removed. The current comparison makes no claim about who receives the transfer or its effect on the poverty headcount.

The jobs chapter uses $3 for weekly hours and $8.30 for the employment, schooling and job-structure splits. Its simulation is an accounting exercise. Changes in group averages do not follow the same households, and the charted associations do not identify policy effects. Every numerical artifact is reconciled separately to its source cells; this does not remove the survey and modelling uncertainties described above.

chartExplainers.title: The Prosperity Gap is 6.72 in Jharkhand and 3.16 in Goa
chartExplainers.takeaway: The 2023-reference-year Prosperity Gap is 6.72 in Jharkhand, 6.31 in Chhattisgarh, 3.91 in Kerala and 3.16 in Goa.
chartExplainers.detail: The index averages each person's ratio of $28 to their daily consumption in 2021 PPP dollars. Lower-consumption households receive more weight. The state scores use the atlas's 2023 reference year, tied to HCES 2023-24.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Maps differences in the depth of consumption shortfalls without choosing a binary poverty cutoff.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Read the map's printed scale and ranked state values: higher scores indicate larger average shortfall ratios. The map is sequential, not a split around the national average.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The score is not $28 divided by a state's mean consumption. It is not a uniform multiplier that would bring every resident to $28.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use the ranked values alongside the map to compare states and union territories.

chartExplainers.title: Young children are more likely to live below $8.30 a day in every state and union territory
chartExplainers.takeaway: Young children are more likely to live in low-consumption households than the average resident of their state.
chartExplainers.detail: SPID records a higher $8.30 poverty share among ages 0-5 than among all ages in all 36 states and union territories. Kerala’s shares are 75.8% and 58.5%; Maharashtra’s are 91.0% and 82.0%. The chart shows 14 selected states.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: A state average hides differences in the households where children grow up. This adds an age comparison to the map’s geographical one.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Open circles show each state’s all-age poverty share; solid dots show the share among ages 0-5. Both use SPID’s direct HCES 2023-24 estimates and the same $8.30 line.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: All ages includes the children, so these are nested groups. Household per-capita consumption does not reveal what children receive within the home. These survey estimates differ from the GSAP calendar lineup used for the map.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Compare the two dots within a state; do not read them as mutually exclusive populations.

chartExplainers.title: The 2021 PPP revision paradox: Updating global prices raised India's 2023 extreme poverty rate to 2.57% while cutting $4.20 poverty to 16.12%
chartExplainers.takeaway: Switching from 2017 PPP to 2021 PPP raised India's 2023-24 extreme poverty rate (+1.55 points, from 1.02% to 2.57%) while lowering its LMIC poverty rate (-3.79 points, from 19.91% to 16.12%).
chartExplainers.detail: The comparison holds the September 2026 release and survey year fixed while changing PPP vintages and their associated poverty lines. In HCES 2023-24, extreme poverty rises from 1.02% to 2.57%, while the lower-middle-income rate falls from 19.91% to 16.12%. The dollar lines belong to different price bases, so their nominal percentage changes are insufficient to explain the Indian rupee thresholds.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Separates a change in the statistical yardstick from a change in household living standards.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each row compares the exact same Indian survey year under the 2017 PPP line (open circle) and the 2021 PPP line (solid dot) in the September 2026 PIP database.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not compare a 2017 PPP poverty rate ($2.15/day) from an older news article with a 2021 PPP poverty rate ($3.00/day) as a change over time; always hold the PPP vintage constant.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Compare the endpoints within each row. Extreme and lower-middle-income benchmarks move in opposite directions.

chartExplainers.title: Depending on survey adjustment and poverty line, India's 2022-23 poverty rate was anywhere between 2.35% and 25.9%
chartExplainers.takeaway: The published estimates vary because both the poverty line and the treatment of survey comparability change.
chartExplainers.detail: Direct HCES gives 5.25% at $3 and 23.89% at $4.20 in 2022-23. Himanshu, Lanjouw and Schirmer instead impute consumption using earlier surveys and common household characteristics. Their CES-based Tendulkar estimates range from 11.3% to 13.6%; their sector-wide EUS-to-PLFS Rangarajan-equivalent estimate is 25.9%.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Distinguishes disagreement about measuring consumption from disagreement about where to set the poverty line.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar is a point estimate with its poverty line and survey treatment in the label. These are selected model specifications, not endpoints of one confidence interval.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The full range cannot be attributed to questionnaire changes alone. Compare estimates using the same poverty line, and allow for imputation uncertainty and assumptions.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Read each method label before comparing bar lengths. Different lines are answering different poverty questions.

chartExplainers.title: Free public foodgrain and welfare items raise measured rural spending by 3.0%, against 1.2% in urban India
chartExplainers.takeaway: Including specified free welfare goods raises published average monthly spending by Rs 125 in rural India and Rs 82 in urban India.
chartExplainers.detail: MoSPI's HCES 2023-24 press note reports rural MPCE of Rs 4,122 without and Rs 4,247 with imputation, a 3.0% boost. Urban MPCE rises from Rs 6,996 to Rs 7,078, or 1.2%. The published averages do not identify the effect on the poorest households.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Makes the valuation of free goods visible while preserving the distinction between a sector average and a distributional effect.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each row is a sector; columns show monthly rupees per person without and with the imputed value of specified free welfare goods. Both columns share the same rupee unit.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The percentage boost uses without-imputation spending as its denominator. Free health services and education-fee waivers are not imputed here, and this is not the World Bank's exact harmonised welfare aggregate.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Compare the distance between the two spending values within each sector, rather than treating the rural-urban level difference as a transfer effect.

chartExplainers.title: The poorest surveyed tenth gained 13.1% in real consumption between the two comparable HCES rounds
chartExplainers.takeaway: The poorest survey decile gained fastest within the two comparable HCES rounds.
chartExplainers.detail: Average real consumption increased 13.1% for the poorest tenth and declined 2.9% for the richest surveyed tenth. National mean consumption grew 4.7%. This is a change in decile averages, not a change in each decile’s consumption share.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: It shows where measured gains occurred without crossing the older survey-design break.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar compares average real consumption in a decile between HCES 2022-23 and 2023-24. Bars to the right of zero show growth; a bar to the left shows a decline.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These are repeated cross-sections. The same people need not occupy a decile in both rounds, and the richest surveyed tenth is not a complete account of affluent Indians.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Start with the poorest tenth, then compare its growth with the other deciles.

chartExplainers.title: National Accounts spending grew 4.49x since 1977 while survey mean grew 2.09x
chartExplainers.takeaway: From 1977 to 2023, India's real GDP per capita grew 5.70-fold and National Accounts household consumption grew 4.49-fold, but NSS/HCES survey mean consumption grew only 2.09-fold.
chartExplainers.detail: All three series are indexed to their own 1977 value. By 2023, National Accounts household consumption per person is 4.49 times its baseline, while survey mean consumption is 2.09 times its baseline. The divergence flags differences in coverage, valuation, reporting and survey methods; it does not identify a single cause.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Provides an independent consistency check on the growth captured by consumption surveys.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Three lines trace real per-capita growth indexed to 100 in 1977 across the nine Indian survey years in PIP (1977, 1983, 1987, 1993, 2004, 2009, 2011, 2022, and 2023).
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The chart does not prove that all missing consumption belongs to rich households or that the truth lies midway between the lines. Consumption inequality is different from income or wealth inequality.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: The common starting value is 100. Compare relative growth, not the original currency levels.

chartExplainers.title: Between 2003 and 2024, adult employment rates in poor Indian households fell to 58.3% while rising to 57.6% among the non-poor
chartExplainers.takeaway: Over the twenty-one years from 2003 to 2024, poor Indian households (<$8.30/day) dramatically expanded secondary schooling, yet the share of their working-age adults in employment declined from 60.72% to 58.29%.
chartExplainers.detail: Among workers in households below $8.30 a day, the share without secondary education falls from 86.71% to 56.47%. The employment rate among working-age adults in those households falls from 60.72% to 58.29%, while it rises from 50.25% to 57.58% in non-poor households. The chart does not isolate the roles of age, gender or local job availability.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Highlights the central empirical puzzle of Chapter 4 for India: rising schooling in poor families coincided with falling adult employment rates.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Open circles show 2003 levels and solid dots show 2024 levels (in %) for poor (<$8.30/day) and non-poor (>=$8.30/day) households across employment and educational attainment.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Poor and non-poor are groups at each date, not the same households followed over time. Employment rates and workers' education shares also have different denominators.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Compare the top two rows: the Poor employment dot moves left (60.72% to 58.29%), while the Non-poor employment dot moves right (50.25% to 57.58%).

chartExplainers.title: Paid employees below $3/day work 44.1 hours a week, against 44.9 above the line
chartExplainers.takeaway: Paid employees below $3/day work 44.05 hours a week on average, against 44.95 above the line.
chartExplainers.detail: The Box 4.1 comparison uses household poverty status at $3 a person a day. For self-employed and unpaid workers, the corresponding averages are 37.05 and 40.61 hours. These averages describe employed people, not all working-age adults.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Tests whether differences in hours alone can explain low household consumption.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each row is an employment type. The two endpoints show average weekly hours for workers below and above the $3/day household consumption line.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not combine this $3/day split with the $8.30/day job-structure comparisons as though they describe the same poor workers. Hours do not measure effort, hourly pay or job security.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Read each employment type separately. Both endpoints use hours per week.

chartExplainers.title: World Bank simulation: Closing India's employment and worker earnings gaps cuts $8.30 poverty by 22.2 percentage points
chartExplainers.takeaway: In the World Bank's Chapter 4 counterfactual (`DataFig4C_123.dta`), raising poor households' adult employment rates and worker earnings to benchmark levels reduces India's $8.30/day poverty rate from 78.78% to 56.61% (-22.17 percentage points).
chartExplainers.detail: The supplied processed counterfactual combines employment and worker-earnings changes. At $8.30/day, the headcount falls by 22.17 percentage points and the poverty gap falls from 25.73% to 16.64%. At $3/day the headcount changes from 2.28% to 1.14%; the file does not separately identify India's education and sector contributions to the combined change.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Shows both the scale and the limits of the report's combined jobs counterfactual.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The two columns compare baseline and simulated levels. Headcounts are shares of people; poverty gaps average the shortfall across everyone as a percentage of the relevant poverty line. Percentage-point reductions are described in the text, not plotted as levels.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: This is an accounting counterfactual, not a forecast or a costed programme. It does not establish the causal effect of any particular jobs policy.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Focus on the top row: $8.30/day poverty drops from 78.78% to 56.61%, a 22.17 percentage-point reduction.

chartExplainers.title: Monetary poverty and deprivation measure different things: 35.5% of children were stunted in NFHS-5
chartExplainers.takeaway: In HCES 2022-23, the World Bank's multidimensional poverty rate is 17.74%, against 5.25% at the monetary extreme line.
chartExplainers.detail: The chart combines different instruments with explicit vintages: HCES 2022-23 for the MPM, HCES 2023-24 for recent monetary lines, NFHS-5 in 2019-21 for child nutrition, and 2022 health-financing observations. Stunting affects 35.5% of children under five; health-cost hardship affects 30.94% of all people in its separate indicator. These are not simultaneous measurements of the same population.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Shows which forms of deprivation a monetary headcount leaves out.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Each bar is a percentage, but the label supplies its population and survey. Child stunting and underweight use children under five; the other measures use people. Source years differ.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Do not add the bars or infer that a lower monetary rate caused the other outcomes. The MPM excludes health and nutrition; medical hardship is not this article's $3/day poverty measure.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Read the population and vintage beside each bar before comparing its length.

chartExplainers.title: India has lower $3 poverty than Bangladesh and Indonesia, and higher poverty at $8.30
chartExplainers.takeaway: India’s low extreme-poverty share does not imply a similar position at the higher benchmark.
chartExplainers.detail: At $8.30 a day, India’s 2024 headcount is 78.8%, against 68.5% in Bangladesh, 68.1% in Indonesia, 18.2% in Viet Nam and 87.2% in Pakistan. India has a lower $3 share than Bangladesh, Indonesia and Pakistan.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Common thresholds reveal where India’s progress compares well and where wider consumption shortfalls remain.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare countries within the same poverty-line column. All values are percentages of each country’s population, in 2021 PPP prices for calendar year 2024.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These countries are selected Asian comparators, not an exhaustive ranking or one income group. Indonesia is marked actual; the other countries are projections or lineup estimates rather than surveys all conducted in the same year.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use the three repeated line labels to compare the same threshold across countries.

caveats: Calendar-year lineup estimates and direct survey years differ. Values after 2024 in the national trajectories are projections or nowcasts, not additional household surveys.
The societal-poverty series uses direct survey years alongside annual lined-up fixed poverty lines. The comparison preserves their different timing and methods.
HCES redesigned interviews and item lists across survey rounds. Models that bridge the break depend on assumptions; their estimates are not interchangeable with direct survey readings.
The Prosperity Gap averages individual ratios of the prosperity standard to consumption. It is not a multiplier for the average household.
The welfare chart uses published sector averages only. The earlier fractile reconstruction required unfrozen microdata and has been removed.
Nutrition, monetary poverty, multidimensional deprivation and medical hardship use different populations and vintages. Their percentages overlap and cannot be added.
The employment comparisons describe groups at each date; households can move between groups. The combined jobs counterfactual does not identify the causal effect of an intervention.

The consumption-loss exercise is a hypothetical uniform reduction in the same 2024 population bins, not a forecast or household transition probability. Its baseline approximates the national lineup at about 0.1 percentage-point resolution.
Decile growth compares repeated cross-sections in PIP’s explicitly comparable HCES rounds. It does not follow the same households or fully measure affluent Indians.

The child comparison uses SPID direct survey estimates, with nested ages 0-5 and all-age populations. It is separate from the GSAP calendar lineup used for the state map; no national child count is inferred.
The selected Asian comparison holds calendar year and PPP lines fixed, but Indonesia is marked actual and the other four countries projection. These are not all in one income group.

The World Bank publishes two projections for India: the report's lineup nowcast puts $4.20 poverty at 10.24% in 2026, while the October 2026 India brief projects 14.2% from a microsimulation it does not publish. Neither is a measurement.

PIP's comparability field puts India's surveys in separate groups, and the charts join surveys from different groups only with a thin grey link. Changes across those links mix real change with changes in survey design.

Statements by NITI Aayog, SBI Research, the Press Information Bureau and individual researchers are reported as their published claims. They use different poverty lines and treatments of transfers and are not reproduced or ranked here.
